description: Jesteśmy dwuosobowym zespołem z Rzeszowa. Interesuje nas przetwarzanie dźwięku i muzyki, analiza danych, web development i dostępność. Planujemy podjąć wyzwanie The Earth Information Jukebox. Skład jest kompletny – nie szukamy nowych członków.
summary: Earth Jukebox is a web page that lets you hear two NASA maps of the Earth: ocean currents with sea surface temperature, and aerosols. You can explore each one as a flat map or as a rotating globe. You move the mouse, a finger or the arrow keys over the map, and the page plays what is under the pointer. On the ocean map warmer water sounds higher and land sounds lower. On the aerosol map soot, dust, sea salt and sulfates each have their own instrument. Every point is also read out as a short sentence with the name of the place, a word such as "warm" and, on the ocean map, the approximate temperature in °C. We built it mainly for blind and low-vision people, who usually get these maps as a picture they cannot see. To make it easier for them, the page can also be controlled by voice in English or Polish: you press K and say, for example, "go to the Baltic Sea" or "legend". Speech is recognised on the user's device, so the recording is not sent anywhere. A short reading mode fits a braille display. You can switch between a plain mode (one note per move) and a musical mode with a fixed 90 BPM rhythm. A school or a museum can put our map with sound on its own website with two lines of HTML. Everything runs in the browser, with no account and no server.
details:
What it does

The page shows two NASA Scientific Visualization Studio maps: ocean currents with sea surface temperature, and aerosols. You explore a map with the mouse, the arrow keys, touch, a screen reader or your voice. For each point the page plays a sound and gives a short reading: the name of the place (a sea, a part of an ocean or a continent), what is there, and a value. On the ocean map the value is an approximate temperature in °C, on the aerosol map it is the amount of each aerosol type from 0 to 1. The same reading appears as text, can be spoken, and is shown on a gauge for people who cannot hear well.

Each map can be shown as a flat map or as a globe. The globe rotates with the arrow keys, a drag or the voice, the G key switches between the two views and R centres the globe again. The sound and the readings are the same in both views.

A few tools help with the whole map, not just one point. "Vibe" plays six notes that sum up a selected area and says how even it is. "Scan" plays the map from north to south in about 14 seconds, with the left and right speakers standing for west and east. You can also choose how much of the map one sound covers (about 90, 180 or 700 km), zoom in, ask "where am I" to hear the coordinates, and listen to the scale from the lowest to the highest note.

On the first visit the page asks how you use it (screen reader, listening only, low vision, or sighted) and sets text size, contrast, speech and sound for that. A short spoken tutorial then walks you through the first steps. A short reading mode gives only the place and its description, so a reading fits on a braille display. Phones vibrate at coastlines, at the edge of the map and at extreme values. On a computer the same signal is a low 90 Hz buzz in the headphones. The page opens in English, and one button switches the interface, the spoken messages and the voice commands to Polish.

Other websites can show our maps too. Two lines of HTML add an <earth-jukebox> element with the ocean or the aerosol map, in English by default or in Polish with lang="pl". It works with the mouse, touch and keyboard, passes each reading to the screen reader, and reports every value as an event, so the host page can use the readings in its own way. A sample page is in the repository (embed-demo.html).

How it works

The page reads the colour of the map under the pointer from a 9 by 9 pixel window. On the ocean map the hue, from blue to red, becomes a value from 0 to 1, and the NASA colour scale for that map turns it into °C. On the aerosol map we split the colour into four aerosol types with a non-negative least squares fit, and the brightness gives the amount of each. The value is mapped to one of 15 notes of a C minor scale between C4 and C6. Land on the ocean map uses a separate instrument that gets lower further from the coast.

The globe draws the same NASA image as a sphere (orthographic projection on an HTML canvas, without external libraries). A point on the sphere is converted to latitude and longitude and then to a pixel of the flat image, so the colour reading, the sound and the place names work exactly as on the flat map.

All instruments are samples we rendered from the free Surge XT synthesizer. We measured them and corrected the loudness of every sample, so low and high notes sound about equally loud. In the musical mode the ocean has one continuous voice that slides to the next note and pulses at 90 BPM. Where the currents are strong the pulse is twice as dense, and where they are weak it is half as dense. Aerosol types play their notes on every beat, each type gets an accent on its own beat, and their notes are pulled to a C minor seventh chord so they do not clash.

Place names come from our own data: 61 seas, 6 straits, 10 ocean regions and simple outlines of the 7 continents. We checked the map positions against known landmarks such as the Cape of Good Hope, Florida and Cape Horn.

Voice control is optional and works in English and Polish, matching the language you choose for the page. You press K, the page says "Listening" (or "Słucham" in Polish), and the microphone opens only after that. Speech is recognised by the Whisper base model running inside the browser, so the recording never leaves the device. The page understands map commands such as "zoom in", "where am I" or "next map", and "go to" with 297 places (all countries, seas, oceans, currents and continents, and NASA Headquarters). It answers with fixed sentences we wrote ourselves, not with a chatbot. If it almost understood a word, it suggests the closest command. Spoken messages use the Piper neural voice in English or Polish (pre-recorded for fixed Polish messages and generated in the browser for the rest), the browser voice, or the user's screen reader.

Benefits

Blind and low-vision people get the same NASA maps as everyone else, in a form they can explore on their own and at their own pace. A school or a museum can use the page for free to give a colour map a sound and text version. Sighted users get a second way to read a map, the globe shows the data as the planet really looks, and the musical mode works for a talk or an exhibition.

What we want to achieve

Our next step is testing with blind and low-vision users, because so far we have only checked the sound with measurements and by listening ourselves. After that we want to add more NASA datasets and offer the embeddable map to schools, museums and libraries.

Honest limits

Aerosol values are relative (0 to 1), not concentrations, because that image has no numeric scale. On the ocean map the page gives approximate temperatures in °C, estimated from the pixel colour with the colour scale published by NASA for that visualization (0 °C blue, about 25 °C yellow, 32 °C red). Each map is one frame of a model, not a long-term average. Place names and continent borders are approximate. The ocean model has no Baltic or Black Sea, so on that map they sound like land.

Tools

JavaScript (ES modules), HTML5 Canvas, Web Audio API, Web Workers, Custom Elements, Web Speech API and Vibration API. Transformers.js with the Whisper base model and ONNX Runtime Web with the Piper voices, both running in the browser. Python with Pillow and NumPy for sample rendering, loudness measurements and the land mask. Surge XT for the instrument sounds. Node.js test runner with 306 automated tests. GitHub and GitHub Pages for code and hosting. The code was written with the help of an AI coding assistant, described in the AI section.
